text: Of the four NIST phases, Preparation is the only one with zero time pressure. No alert blinking, no executive asking for updates, no clock running. That calm is the whole point: it's the only time a SOC can build its incident response capability deliberately instead of improvising one under pressure, which is exactly why it's the phase most likely to get shortchanged when nobody's watching.

Preparation covers three things, and all three have to exist before the first alert fires, not during it: a written incident response plan, a team that has actually trained on using it, and tools and access that are already provisioned and tested. Skipping any one of them doesn't just slow a team down later — it guarantees the team is improvising exactly when improvising is most dangerous.

A real IR plan names who has authority to take a system offline, authorize contacting law enforcement, or talk to the press, and it defines severity levels so the team isn't debating that mid-incident. Chapter 2 covers exactly what a real plan contains. A trained team has rehearsed the plan through tabletop exercises — simulated incidents walked through step by step — and knows their specific role before an incident starts, not after.

Ready tools and access is what most clearly separates Preparation from scrambling. Imagine an incident starts and the team's first move is isolating a compromised server, but nobody has the admin credentials because the prior admin left two months ago and access was never reassigned. That's not a detection problem or a containment problem. It's a Preparation failure, and it costs real time in the one phase where time matters most.

Real Preparation means the access, the forensic tooling, and the communication channels a team will need are already set up, already tested, and already known to work, long before anyone needs them. Next up: Detection and Analysis, where an alert gets formally confirmed as a real incident and its nature gets understood, at the scale this chapter is building toward.
